title: Review
body:
Step five of [[Software Requirements Analysis]]: sit down with the customer and the
[[Specification]] and confirm that it says what they meant. It is the last checkpoint before
the requirements are treated as settled, and it is cheap: reading a document costs hours,
rebuilding from a misunderstanding costs the project.

The same technique generalises past requirements. A **code review** or **design review** is
one or more people reading the artefact looking for problems, with no machine involved. That
matters because reviews catch a class of defect that testing structurally cannot:

- a requirement that was misunderstood (the tests encode the same misunderstanding)
- [[Code Smells]] and [[Coupling and Cohesion]] problems, which are not failures at all
- missing cases nobody thought to test

[[Unit testing]] catches "this does not do what the author intended". Review catches "the
author intended the wrong thing". Neither substitutes for the other, and finding a defect in
review puts it at the cheapest point on the [[SDLC]] cost curve.

The rule that makes reviews work is that you review the artefact, not the author. A review
that turns into a defence of the code stops finding anything.
